title: What is S3 versioning, how does it protect against accidental overwrite/delete (delete markers), and how does it combine with lifecycle rules and MFA delete?
shortTitle: S3 Versioning, Delete Markers, Lifecycle, and MFA Delete
keyPoints: S3 versioning keeps every version of an object so accidental overwrites and deletes are fully recoverable.
Deleting an object in a versioned bucket inserts a delete marker instead of erasing data, and removing the marker restores the object.
Permanently erasing data requires deleting a specific version ID, which is a deliberate separate operation.
Lifecycle rules target noncurrent versions to transition or expire them, controlling cost without losing the current version.
MFA Delete requires a multi-factor authentication code to permanently delete a version or disable versioning, guarding against compromised credentials.
Versioning cannot be turned off once enabled, only suspended, and suspended keeps existing versions but stops creating new ones.
For true WORM compliance, Object Lock in compliance mode is preferred over MFA Delete alone.

s1_definition.oneliner: Versioning keeps every version and uses a delete marker instead of erasing, so accidental overwrites and deletes are recoverable, while lifecycle rules clean up old versions and MFA Delete guards permanent deletion.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **S3 versioning** – a bucket-level setting that keeps every version of an object instead of overwriting it; each PUT creates a new version with a unique version ID while older versions are retained.
- **Delete marker** – when you delete an object in a versioned bucket, S3 inserts a delete marker that hides the object rather than erasing data; removing the marker restores the object.
- **Noncurrent versions** – previous versions that are no longer the current one; lifecycle rules can transition or expire them independently.
- **MFA Delete** – a setting that requires a multi-factor authentication code to permanently delete a version or disable versioning.
- **Object Lock** – a complementary feature that provides write-once-read-many (WORM) compliance in governance or compliance mode.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a customer's KYC document. Without versioning, if a clerk uploads a wrong file over the right one, the original is gone forever. With versioning, the warehouse keeps every copy ever filed, stamped with a version number, so the old correct copy is still there. If someone "deletes" the document, the warehouse does not shred it -- it just puts a "hidden" sticker (a delete marker) on top, and a supervisor can peel off the sticker to get the document back. Lifecycle rules are the warehouse policy that shreds very old hidden copies to save space, and MFA Delete is the rule that permanently shredding anything requires two keys turned at once by an authorized manager.

sections.s6_takeaway:
S3 versioning is a bucket-level setting that keeps every version of an object rather than overwriting it. Each upload to the same key creates a new current version with a unique version ID, and previous versions are retained as noncurrent versions that you can still read by their IDs. This is the foundation of protecting data against accidental changes.

The clever part is how deletion works. On a versioned bucket a normal delete does not erase anything; it writes a delete marker that becomes the current version, so a plain read returns a 404 as if the object is gone, but the real data sits underneath. To recover, you delete the delete marker by its version ID and the previous version becomes current again. To genuinely erase data you must delete a specific version ID, which is a deliberate, separate action.

Versioning combines with lifecycle rules and MFA Delete to stay safe and affordable. Keeping every version forever is expensive, so I write lifecycle rules that target noncurrent versions specifically, transitioning them to cheaper classes and expiring them after a safe period, and cleaning up expired delete markers and incomplete uploads. MFA Delete adds a hard safeguard: permanently deleting a version or disabling versioning requires a multi-factor code from the root account's device, so even stolen credentials cannot wipe the audit history. For true WORM compliance, Object Lock in compliance mode is even stronger because nobody, not even root, can delete a locked object before its retention expires.

At National Bank of India we stored KYC documents in a versioned S3 bucket. When a clerk overwrote Rajesh's correct PAN card with the wrong file, the original was still there as a noncurrent version and I restored it in seconds. I set a lifecycle rule to expire noncurrent versions after ninety days to control cost, and protected the bucket with Object Lock in compliance mode for regulatory retention.

Remember one sentence: S3 versioning keeps every version and uses delete markers instead of erasing, so accidental overwrites and deletes are fully recoverable, and lifecycle rules on noncurrent versions keep the cost under control.
